SCHTEACH.TITLE: Intro to Manuf Engineering
SCHTEACH.SYLLABUS: edna.orozco01/schteach/MANE1101 ABET Syllabus Intro to Manufacturing Engineering Spring 2026-1.docx
SCHTEACH.PEDINN: Pedagogical innovations in this Introduction to Engineering course emphasized project-based, experiential, and ethics-centered learning aligned with ABET Student Outcomes. Students applied the engineering design process through hands-on CAD modeling, prototyping, reverse engineering, and a team-based catapult and CNC-focused project, directly supporting SO (1) problem solving and SO (2) engineering design. Computer-based tools, including CAD software, spreadsheet analysis, and introductory manufacturing platforms, were integrated to strengthen SO (1) and SO (7). Ethical reasoning and professional responsibility were addressed through case studies and group discussions aligned with the NSPE Code of Ethics, supporting SO (4). Team-based projects, structured collaboration, and presentations reinforced SO (5) teamwork and SO (3) communication skills, while exposure to multiple engineering disciplines and modern tools promoted awareness of contemporary engineering practice and lifelong learning (SO (6)
SCHTEACH.TECHMAT: During the current year, new teaching materials were developed to support hands-on, industry-aligned learning in Introduction to Engineering. These included instructor-created CAD tutorials, step-by-step modeling modules, and guided laboratory handouts for prototyping, CNC exposure, and reverse-engineering activities. In preparation for an industry-recognized CNC certification, custom instructional modules, practice exercises, and assessment materials were implemented in alignment with America’s Cutting Edge (ACE) and Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station (TEES) certification standards. Additional materials such as project rubrics, milestone checklists, presentation templates, short instructional videos, and quiz banks were developed to support team-based projects and ensure consistent, skills-based assessment.
SCHTEACH.ENHSTUD: Several course activities were implemented to enhance student learning and engagement with the broader engineering community. Students participated in team-based, hands-on design and manufacturing projects that emphasized real-world problem solving, collaboration, and communication. Guest speakers from industry and engineering-related organizations were invited to discuss career pathways, professional expectations, and the societal impact of engineering. Ethical case studies and discussions were contextualized using examples relevant to community needs and engineering practice. Collaborative projects and presentations fostered peer learning and introduced students to professional communication with diverse audiences, supporting early professional identity formation and community awareness.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Track 4 - Phase II: Center for Broadening Participation in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich, Examine (CBPE-E4)
NSF Center for Equity in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich (CEE-E3)
Broadening Participation in STEM
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is located in the historic Texan borderlands created at the end of the Mexican-American war in 1848 which separated families on both sides of the Rio Grande River. The university was formed in 2013 when The University of Texas at Brownsville and The University of Texas Pan-American were consolidated to expand educational opportunities in the underserved and rural Valley of the Rio Grande. UTRGV is a major Hispanic-Serving Institution (HSI), primarily a nonresidential, 4-year, public, R2 institution, with campuses situated along the lower 100 miles of the Rio Grande. UTRGV's student demographics mirror those of the Lower Rio Grande Valley (RGV), with over 95% of our 32,000 students being of Hispanic or Latinx origin (Region One Education Service Center, 2021), and over 85% having Mexican-American heritage. Academic programs in engineering, started in 1992, were first accredited by ABET in 1996. The College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) currently has 6 departments offering 8 bachelors' and 7 masters' degrees. The college has over 110 faculty members and serves nearly 3900 students, mostly (90%) undergraduates. Although CECS does not have a PhD program yet, a pathway for a doctoral degree is offered jointly with the University of Nebraska at Lincoln (UNL). As the second largest HSI in the nation, UTR V is uniquely positioned to broaden the participation of Hispanics in the engineering workforce.
CONGRANT.OTHER_AGENCIES: The proposal focuses on increasing “effective STEM education and broadening participation” in underrepresented minority STEM students at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) to successfully face academic and professional challenges, recently exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The Freshman Year Innovator Experience proposes the development of self-transformation skills in freshman mechanical engineering students to successfully face academic and professional challenges exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic while working on two parallel projects of technical design innovation and academic career pathways.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Improving Undergraduate STEM Education by Changing Institutional Culture
CONGRANT.SPONORG: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Contextualization

Families in the Rio Grande Valley, like other minority groups, have historically been exploited, dominated, acculturated, subjugated, and marginalized socially, culturally, linguistically and educationally (Valencia, 2010). Such historical realities have kept Hispanic families, and other groups underrepresented in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) from finding a true sense of belonging, even after living in the region(s) for generations. The creation of The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV), founded with values and beliefs that are culturally responsive to the communities it serves, presents greater opportunities for Hispanic families and communities and other minorities underrepresented in higher education, especially in STEM disciplines (e.g., first generation, females, international, transfer, commuting, and non-English speaking). Since its establishment in 2015, UTRGV has made significant leaps in research, teaching, and service. Student success has been at its center for countless initiatives.

Even though several initiatives have had significant gains in desired academic and non-academic outcomes, none has had a broader impact than the current NSF funded initiative HSI Institutional Transformation Project: Improving Undergraduate STEM Education Through Family-Centered Pedagogy (award number 2122875). This program impacted over 1,200 undergraduate students enrolled in Physics, Chemistry, and Mathematics courses in the 2022-2023 academic year. We observed increased engagement and participation from STEM undergraduate students, with the support of over 300 families from underrepresented communities in the RGV. Moreover, in a survey conducted at the end of the semester symposium, most students, their families, AVE Frontera family leaders, and STEM faculty reported experiencing a strong sense of belonging with ownership and pride. They noted that this was an event where families from the local community came together to support STEM students in a family-friendly, family-integrated learning environment at UTRGV. The preliminary data observed at UTRGV suggests that the proposed project has the potential to shed new light to “sense of belonging with ownership and pride” and Institutional Social Responsibility (Salinas, 2018) among Hispanic students, families and other underrepresented communities in STEM.

Theoretical Framework

Our theoretical framework encompasses: 1) a novel Family-Centered Theory of Change that addresses diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI); and 2) an intersectionality lens used to guide and assess the transformational impact on teaching and learning, curricula, student success, assessment, and pedagogical practices in undergraduate physics, mathematics, and chemistry courses. The proposed project benefits from the relational partnership between leaders from an institution of higher education, UTRGV, and leaders from a community-based organization, AVE Frontera. AVE (A Vehicle of Engagement) Frontera is a grassroots advocacy group that serves as a vehicle of engagement that is family-centered, instills cultural pride and awareness amongst its members, and fulfills their physical, emotional, social, spiritual, and intellectual needs. The Family-Centered Model brings stakeholders in a process of sustainable knowledge co-production (Norström et al., 2020) allowing students, families from the community, faculty, and researchers to co-develop pedagogical and research practices impacting engaged student learning and institutional culture change. The goal of the proposed project is twofold: 1) to create a sustainable institutional culture of mentorship in STEM research; and 2) to create a sustainable institutional culture of engaged student learning in STEM.


Family-Centered Project Activities

Activities for Goal 1
Project efforts will go towards creating a sustainable institutional culture of mentorship in STEM Research. The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) was founded in 2015, through the merger of the two legacy institutions: University of Texas Pan American and University of Texas Brownsville (both legacy institutions serving the Rio Grande Valley Region [RGV] of South Texas), as a Doctoral/Professional University and has since worked towards the goal of becoming an R1 University. In 2019 UTRGV went from a Doctoral/Professional University to becoming an R2 University and continues to aim towards becoming an R1 university. Through the Family-Centered Model, we plan to foster a culture of mentorship in STEM Research that will strengthen STEM education at UTRGV as well as support UTRGV’s goal of becoming an R1 institution.

The STEM faculty participating in the undergraduate research mentoring will:

Mentor/train the undergraduate students in research skills;Generate family-friendly environments where students’ family members arewelcomed to participate in research activity discussions;
Be open to exploring valid and reasonable options of incorporating interestedstudents’ family members into the research endeavor;
As PI submit and develop a research proposal by the end of the year;The submitted proposal will include active collaboration of the participatingundergraduate students and their families, including proposal writing.

Activities for Goal #2
Project efforts will also go towards creating a sustainable institutional culture of engaged student learning in STEM. We will also have one convocation (mini-conference) per semester where participating faculty, students, and students’ families can meet, share experiences and present results. The convocations will be open to culturally relevant, community-engaged, and/or family-centered pedagogy scholars, and to all interested students (goal is 75-100 participants). We will also have one summer student-workshop per year for the participating students to explore future graduate studies and work options, to help students prepare for graduate school applications, and to prepare CVs for private sector job applications.

By establishing undergraduate student/faculty teams, faculty will be encouraged to incorporate undergraduate students to research endeavor nurturing an engaged learning environment. By fostering a family-friendly environment, the undergraduate student will be more motivated to pursue research at undergraduate levels and additionally it also produces a stronger support from the families for the student to pursue a STEM research career, that in turn should increase student retention rates in STEM. The grant-preparing experience gained by the undergraduate student will also prepare the student for future graduate studies and beyond. Further, with a fraction of the total proposal submitted approved, this will motivate faculty to continue incorporating undergraduate students in research efforts as well gain the support of Departmental and College administration for these efforts leading to sustainability.

The Research and Mentoring effort of this project will directly impact fourteen STEM faculty and twenty-eight STEM students. Of course, in nurturing a sustainable culture of mentorship in STEM Research that actively incorporates undergraduate students, we expect the impact to be much larger (60 STEM faculty, 200 students) over the duration of the project, supporting our colleges and university efforts towards becoming an R1 institution.

CONGRANT.TITLE: PATH-2-STARS: Pathway to Advance Training of Hispanics 2 Succeed Through Active Research/Education on Space

INTELLCONT.TITLE: NSF EEC: Establishing UTRGV's Center for Broadening Participation in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Hispanics are one of the fastest growing populations in the US, yet they are underrepresented in engineering. University X, a major Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI) with a student population over 95% Hispanic, is well-positioned to address this disparity. University X established a Center for Broadening Participation in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich (CBPE-E3) to enhance Hispanic participation in engineering from early awareness through professional employment. The CBPE -E3 aims to increase enrollment, retention, and advancement rates of Hispanic students in higher education engineering, especially Latinas facing intersectional barriers of race and gender. The CBPE -E3 envisions becoming the leading national model for inclusion, professional preparation, and successful advancement of Hispanic engineers. Drawing on the community wealth asset framework, the CBPE -E3 is grounded in culturally relevant programming and pedagogy. It encompasses three objectives and related focus areas: 1) ENGAGE (K-12 Outreach): Provide early exposure to engineering content and role models for students, their families and communities, and teachers and counselors; 2) EDUCATE (Education & Training): Create an inclusive college experience that promotes students' success through curricular reform and trainings for faculty and students; and 3) ENRICH (Professional & Research Experiences): Provide the next generation of engineers with critical professional, leadership, and research development opportunities. The CBPE -E3 builds on University X's long-standing commitment to supporting Latinx students, as recognized with a 2021 Seal of Excelencia, and in broadening participation through successful NSF ADVANCE IT, INCLUDES, and ECR grants. It also leverages partnerships with 14 entities, including major universities, engineering professional societies, community colleges, K-12 systems, non-profits, and engineering employers and alumni. The CBPE -E3 expands University X's student educational opportunities through an R1 institution collaboration to create the Alliance for Student Participation in Research Experiences for Hispanics (ASPIRE Hispanics). It also introduces students to role models, professional networks, and ongoing personal and career development through professional society partners. Finally, the CBPE -E3 shares promising practices with institutions serving largely Hispanic populations so that they can replicate or adapt best practices at their home campuses through an "Equity in Engineering Education Summit." Infrastructure in phase I will be expanded for national scale-up in phase II. The authors will present the work in progress and preliminary results from a pilot implementation. This project is funded by NSF award 2217780.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Work in Progress: Development of A Boostcamp for Freshman Student Success During COVID-19 Transition
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Assessment results show that passing rates in introductory courses and retention rates of first-year students in the College of Engineering and Computer Science at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, a predominantly Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI), significantly dropped with the onset of COVID-19. These results and trends highlight the academic preparation of incoming students, particularly the new cohort of underrepresented Hispanic students from underserved and challenged communities in the region, who may not have sufficiently develop the necessary skills (e.g., adaptability, persistence, and performance) for the rigor of engineering education. To address this challenge, an onboarding “boostcamp” was created for incoming and transfer students to bridge the transition from secondary education to higher education. The boostcamp primes students to overcome academic deficiencies, develop a critical skills portfolio, learn problem-solving techniques, build a sustainable community of mentoring support with faculty and students, and gain a template to sustain academic and professional success during their undergraduate education. The paper presents the boostcamp's design process steps, including curricular analysis, identification of areas for improvement, skills inventory, and blueprinting, as well as its initial implementation in the mechanical engineering program. The boostcamp was organized over a week and featured hands-on engineering activities, faculty and student talks, and engineering lab tours. It was based on a design thinking approach and structured around Challenge-based Instruction, innovation, design, and mentoring. Daily activities focused on promoting critical thinking, assertiveness in the face of adversity, informed decision-making, and task prioritization. Results indicate that the boostcamp increased student confidence and established a valuable network system among participants. Future work will focus on expanding the boostcamp to include students from other engineering and computer science departments and developing a template for other institutions with similar challenges.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: At-Risk Freshmen Student Retention After STEM Intervention
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Internal Journal of Arts, Humanities and Social Studies
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Background: Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) areas are one of the fastest-growing majors in the nation. Engineering is projected to add the second largest number of new jobs from 2016 to 2026 with 140,000 new jobs (Torpey, 2018).According to the National Center for Education Statistics despite all the research done throughout decades to improve the issue of retention in STEM areas about half of the students who pursue a degree in STEM will either leave or change majors. Purpose: This study aimed to sample at-risk college freshmen students from the College of Engineering & Computer Science, to describe and explain the association between retention after the first year of at-risk college freshmen students in a STEM program and completion of a STEM intervention, to identify the reasons STEM students decided to stay in the program after completing a STEM intervention, and to identify how to improve the STEM intervention. Method: A Chi-square test of independence was used to find if there was an association between the completion of a STEM intervention and the retention rate of at-risk freshmen students and focus group interviews. Results & Conclusions: The quantitative analysis, a test of independence X2 (chi-square)found no statistically significant association between STEM intervention completion and retention. The qualitative analysis provided five themes describing the students’ STEM intervention experience was also provided: learning activities and processes, mentorship, sense of belonging, and transitioning from high school to college.

Rocking the Syllabus: Innovative Ways to Make Your Syllabus Student-Centered and Engaging
PRESENT.ABSTRACT:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HYy4YtATr4c&feature=emb_imp_woyt

Your course syllabus provides students with their first impression of your class. Learn how to wow them with a syllabus that is dynamic, engaging, practical, and student-centered. Our panelists will share how they revised their syllabi to make them more inviting, inclusive, and useful in order to set the tone for a positive learning environment and a great semester.

Purpose
-To help colleagues consider revisions to their syllabuses that will increase document usability and student understanding of the course
-Using the syllabus as a tool to create a positive and engaging learning environment even before class begins
-To help faculty develop a syllabus that conveys course requirements, course guidelines, important dates, and other vital information more effectively by considering the student's needs and expectations. (ORE)
-To help faculty transition the newly developed syllabus to the online environment by creating a FAQ section on Blackboard. (ORE)

Learning Objectives
-To examine the information of their current syllabus to identify significant information for the students (ORE)
-Assemble a list of significant information for the students such as important dates, resources, procedures, and other course requirements (ORE)
-Construct a list of three strategies learned from the workshop, such as student centered language, video incorporation, embedded links, web links, images, colors, snapshots, icons, bilingual text or student advice, to immediately apply into a newly developed syllabus. (ORE)
